subject: Neurology
vignette: A medical student examines a diagram of the motor and sensory homunculus. She is struck that the lips, tongue, thumb, and fingers occupy disproportionately large areas, while the trunk and lower limb occupy relatively small areas.
question: What best explains the distorted appearance of the cortical homunculus?

options.text: Body regions with richer innervation have a larger cortical representation
The homunculus is drawn proportional to the physical size of each body part
Larger muscles always occupy more cortex regardless of innervation
The lower extremity is overrepresented because of its role in gait
Cortical representation is uniform across all body regions

explanation_correct: The homunculus is a topographic representation of motor and sensory areas in the cerebral cortex. Its distorted appearance reflects the fact that more richly innervated body regions (for example, lips, tongue, thumb, and fingers) have a greater cortical representation, not because of their physical size.

explanation_incorrect.B: The homunculus is not proportional to the physical size of body parts; the hands and face are greatly enlarged.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cortical representation depends on innervation density rather than simply muscle size.
explanation_incorrect.D: The lower extremity is relatively underrepresented compared with the hand and face.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cortical representation is decidedly nonuniform, with fine-movement and highly sensitive regions enlarged.

educationalObjective: Explain that homuncular distortion reflects innervation density rather than body size.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 60-year-old man suffers severe hypotension during cardiac surgery. Imaging shows an infarct in the cortical border zone between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Postoperatively, he has weakness of both proximal upper extremities while lower extremity strength is preserved.
question: Which of the following best describes this patient's "man-in-a-barrel" syndrome?

options.text: PCA-MCA watershed infarct causing higher-order visual dysfunction
ACA infarct causing contralateral leg-predominant weakness
ACA-MCA watershed infarct causing proximal upper extremity weakness sparing the lower extremities
MCA infarct causing contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia
Internal border-zone infarct causing isolated hand weakness

explanation_correct: Cortical watershed (border) zones occur between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries and between the posterior and middle cerebral arteries. An ACA-MCA watershed infarct due to severe hypoperfusion produces proximal upper extremity weakness with sparing of the lower extremities, the "man-in-a-barrel" syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: PCA-MCA watershed infarcts cause higher-order visual dysfunction, not proximal upper extremity weakness.
explanation_incorrect.B: An ACA territory infarct causes contralateral leg-predominant weakness, not the proximal-arm pattern described.
explanation_incorrect.D: An MCA territory infarct causes contralateral face and arm weakness and aphasia if dominant, not this watershed pattern.
explanation_incorrect.E: Internal border-zone infarcts lie between MCA superficial and deep territories and typically cause hand and arm weakness, not the classic man-in-a-barrel distribution.

educationalObjective: Relate ACA-MCA watershed infarcts to proximal upper extremity ("man-in-a-barrel") weakness.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 68-year-old woman has severe hypotension after a bleeding ulcer. Imaging reveals an infarct in the border zone between the posterior and middle cerebral arteries. She has difficulty with higher-order visual processing, including recognizing and interpreting what she sees, despite relatively preserved basic visual acuity.
question: Which deficit is most characteristic of a PCA-MCA watershed infarct?

options.text: Proximal upper extremity weakness sparing the legs
Contralateral leg weakness with urinary incontinence
Broca aphasia with intact comprehension
Ipsilateral facial weakness and hyperacusis
Higher-order visual dysfunction

explanation_correct: A PCA-MCA watershed infarct due to severe hypoperfusion produces higher-order visual dysfunction. These cortical border zones lie between the posterior and middle cerebral artery territories, regions involved in visual association processing; basic visual acuity may be relatively preserved while complex visual interpretation is impaired.

explanation_incorrect.A: Proximal upper extremity weakness sparing the legs is the ACA-MCA watershed "man-in-a-barrel" syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.B: Contralateral leg weakness with incontinence suggests an anteromedial ACA territory infarct, not a PCA-MCA watershed infarct.
explanation_incorrect.C: Broca aphasia reflects an inferior frontal (MCA superior division) lesion, not a watershed visual deficit.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ipsilateral facial weakness and hyperacusis suggest a peripheral facial nerve (Bell palsy) lesion, not a cortical watershed infarct.

educationalObjective: Associate PCA-MCA watershed infarcts with higher-order visual dysfunction.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A radiologist reviews a brain MRI and wants to confirm the vascular territories. She recalls that the anterior cerebral artery supplies the anteromedial surface, the middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface, and the posterior cerebral artery supplies the posterior and inferior surfaces. Watershed (border) zones are also common sites of brain metastases.
question: Which of the following correctly matches a cerebral artery with its cortical distribution?

options.text: ACA - lateral surface; MCA - anteromedial surface; PCA - posterior/inferior surface
ACA - posterior/inferior surface; MCA - lateral surface; PCA - anteromedial surface
ACA - anteromedial surface; MCA - posterior/inferior surface; PCA - lateral surface
ACA - anteromedial surface; MCA - lateral surface; PCA - posterior and inferior surfaces
ACA, MCA, and PCA each supply the anteromedial surface equally

explanation_correct: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the anteromedial cortical surface, the middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface, and the posterior cerebral artery supplies the posterior and inferior surfaces. Cortical border (watershed) zones between these territories are common locations for brain metastases.

explanation_incorrect.A: This swaps the ACA and MCA territories; ACA is anteromedial and MCA is lateral.
explanation_incorrect.B: This incorrectly assigns the posterior/inferior surface to the ACA and the anteromedial surface to the PCA.
explanation_incorrect.C: This incorrectly assigns the lateral surface to the PCA and the posterior/inferior surface to the MCA.
explanation_incorrect.E: The three arteries have distinct principal cortical territories rather than all supplying the anteromedial surface equally.

educationalObjective: Match ACA, MCA, and PCA to their principal cortical distributions and note that watershed zones are common metastasis sites.
